task.goal: Create a short participatory rhythm piece for a ferry terminal lounge using silent or near-silent gestures.
hard_constraints: No amplified sound, tapping on fixtures, blocking boarding signs or interrupting announcements.
Travelers can join or leave without being singled out and may participate seated.
A single facilitator must set up and clear the activity within ten minutes; test comfort with observation and an optional question.
task.available_resources: Printed gesture cards, portable sign and terminal staff's permitted corner.
task.expected_result: Distinct working forms and a reversible one-session pilot.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A shared visual pulse
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: a facilitator provides a visible beat that travelers can follow without making sound. In the staff-permitted corner, display a portable sign reading: “Quiet rhythm—watch or join, seated or standing; stop whenever you like. Announcements take priority.” Printed cards show a four-beat phrase: open palm, close palm, open palm, rest. For two minutes, the facilitator repeats these small gestures at chest height, then finishes by lowering both hands. Travelers may mirror with one hand or make smaller finger movements; watching is equally welcome. There are no solos, invitations directed at individuals, or corrections.

The common visual reference could produce a recognizable ensemble rhythm without anyone needing to hear or memorize instructions. The outcome depends mainly on whether the pulse is easy to see and comfortably paced. It assumes staff approve the location and the facilitator remains visible without covering boarding information. Limited sightlines and visual or hand-movement impairments may restrict participation. Use only the cards and sign; allow three minutes to position them, two minutes for the piece, and two minutes to clear. Immediately lower hands during announcements and restart only afterward.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Pilot one two-minute phrase, comparing its first four repetitions with a simpler repeated open-palm/rest pattern. The facilitator observes whether willing participants can follow, remain seated, and leave freely, without recording identities. Offer a printed optional question: “Was this comfortable to watch or join?” Abandon the more complex phrase if it produces repeated searching, visible strain, or less coordinated participation than the simple pulse. Stop the pilot immediately if staff identify distraction or access problems. Coordination alone does not establish comfort; silence is not consent.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Choose-your-own counter-rhythm
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: independent repeating patterns overlap, creating a quiet rhythm piece without requiring travelers to synchronize with a leader. Display three printed gesture scores beside the portable sign: A—turn one palm up, rest, turn it down, rest; B—extend one finger, extend a second, relax; C—slowly open a hand, then pause. Each person chooses a comfortable pace and any score, changing or stopping freely. All movements stay within the participant’s own seated space, without touching fixtures or producing deliberate sound.

The facilitator demonstrates each pattern once, then performs one continuously for a three-minute session. The sign explains that overlapping cycles are the piece: matching other people is optional. Different cycle lengths and self-selected tempos create changing visual combinations. This could reduce the pressure of keeping up while preserving repetition and rests as rhythmic material. It assumes travelers can understand the cards without individual instruction and that a small cluster is visible from existing lounge seats. The result may resemble scattered movement rather than a shared composition; that uncertainty is central to the pilot. The facilitator needs three minutes to place the cards and sign and two minutes to clear them. Announcements suspend the activity, as stated on the sign and modeled by the facilitator.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare a short opening in which everyone may use pattern A with the subsequent choice of three patterns. Observe whether choice allows continued, apparently relaxed participation or instead causes hesitation and repeated card-checking. Present the optional question: “Was choosing your own pattern comfortable, or would one shared pattern be easier?” Treat sparse participation as inconclusive. Simplify to one pattern if choice consistently confuses willing participants; discontinue if movements distract from announcements or boarding.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A rhythm read across the page
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: a printed visual score carries the timing, allowing each traveler to perform a complete miniature privately rather than follow people. One large gesture card shows eight evenly spaced symbols: open hand, rest, two fingers, rest, open hand, two fingers, rest, rest. The instruction is: “Read left to right at your own comfortable walking pace. Repeat up to three times, or stop anywhere.” Symbols include short text labels. Participants may use tiny finger movements with a hand resting on their lap; no clapping, snapping, fixture contact, or coordinated breathing is requested.

The facilitator places the score and portable invitation sign in the permitted corner, silently demonstrates one reading, and leaves a three-minute window for people to try it whenever they wish. Each independent reading has a beginning, repeated motif, and long ending rest. This makes the printed sequence itself the organizing device, potentially accommodating late arrivals and departures without exposing anyone as out of time. It assumes the score is legible from permitted seats; travelers should never need to crowd around it. It offers less collective synchrony than a conducted piece, and visual accessibility remains a limit. Setup takes three minutes and removal two. The sign explicitly says to pause for announcements, with the facilitator immediately modeling that pause.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: During one session, first display a four-symbol version—open hand, rest, two fingers, rest—then the eight-symbol score. Observe from the corner whether willing readers can complete either without approaching the sign, seeking explanation, or visibly losing their place. Offer the optional question: “Was the card comfortable to follow from your seat?” Retain the longer score only if it remains readable and its ending is understandable. If neither works from existing seats, end the pilot rather than reposition travelers or enlarge the activity into circulation space.

DIRECT_FULL.title: The lounge answers itself
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: a delayed visual feedback loop generates the rhythm. Travelers show the opposite of the facilitator’s hand; the facilitator periodically copies the group’s most common gesture. Each collective response therefore changes the next cue. The facilitator follows the participants’ visible choices rather than conducting a predetermined sequence.

In the staff-permitted corner, place a portable sign and two printed cards: “When my hand is open, loosely curl yours; when mine is curled, open yours.” Add: “Watching counts. Join or stop anytime; stay seated if you wish. Announcements mean hands down.” No gripping, clapping, snapping, or contact with fixtures is involved. Participants can keep one hand near their lap. The facilitator never addresses individuals or asks anyone to raise a hand higher.

Begin with an open hand. After roughly three seconds, copy whichever gesture is more common among clearly visible participating hands; repeat for up to ninety seconds. If the group is evenly divided or no participating hands are visible, lower the hand and end. Alternating responses should create a slow visual rhythm whose continuation depends on voluntary participation.

This requires enough willing participants within comfortable sightlines to make the aggregate readable. It may fail because inversion is confusing, hands are hard to see, or people feel watched. Do not scan faces, count individuals publicly, or interpret watching as participation. Keep boarding signs and circulation clear; immediately suspend the piece during announcements. One facilitator needs only the supplied materials: three minutes to set up, up to three minutes for demonstration and activity, and two minutes to clear. Removing the materials fully reverses the pilot.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Within one session, demonstrate twenty seconds of ordinary same-gesture mirroring, then explain and try the feedback version. Observe whether several successive exchanges remain readable without individual prompting, louder instructions, or larger movements. Offer the optional printed question: “Which felt more comfortable: copying, showing the opposite, or neither?” If the feedback version repeatedly stalls, requires coaching, or attracts reports of scrutiny, reject it in favor of the simple comparator. Stop for any staff concern about announcements or access. Successful alternation would show feasibility, not establish comfort; sparse participation leaves the result uncertain.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A phrase becomes a rhythm
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Mechanism: travelers turn the stress pattern of a familiar phrase into small, silent gestures. Language supplies the rhythm: silently imagine saying a short phrase, gently extend one finger on its emphasized syllables, then relax the hand for a pause. Repeat twice if comfortable. No whispering, audible breath, tapping, or contact with fixtures is needed. A hand may remain on the lap throughout.

In the staff-permitted corner, the facilitator displays a printed example with emphasized words: “WELCOME aboard; TIME to REST.” The card explains that this is one possible reading; travelers may use any familiar phrase in any language, without disclosing it. The portable sign reads: “Silent phrase rhythms. Watch or try from your seat. Join or stop whenever you like. Pause completely for announcements.” The facilitator demonstrates with finger movements and a second hand tracing the printed example, without speaking or mouthing words.

The changing pattern of emphasis generates each miniature, rather than a leader’s beat or a prescribed gesture sequence. Familiar wording could make a rhythm easier to remember and give it personal character. Participants need not synchronize or reveal their choices, and no individual is invited, corrected, or asked to demonstrate.

This assumes the instructions are readable from existing seats and that participants can comfortably imagine a phrase and move a finger. Speech rhythms vary, and some phrases may produce little recognizable repetition; that is acceptable unless the activity becomes confusing. The facilitator needs only the supplied cards and sign: three minutes to set up, a two-minute participation window, and two minutes to clear. Keep circulation and boarding information clear, and immediately suspend gestures during announcements. Removing the materials reverses the session.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: During the single session, offer a simple comparator first: silently imagine four evenly spaced counts and extend one finger on each. Then display the phrase method. Observe whether willing participants can attempt either from their seats without approaching for explanation or showing apparent strain; do not track individuals or interpret stillness as discomfort. Offer the optional printed question: “Which felt more comfortable: counts, a phrase, or neither?” Reject the phrase method if willing respondents repeatedly find the translation confusing or uncomfortable relative to counting. Sparse participation leaves feasibility uncertain. Stop immediately for staff concerns about access or distraction; successful gestures alone do not establish comfort.

EXPAND.title: A ripple that travels and expires
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: participants pass a small gesture onward, so local handoffs create the rhythm without a shared beat or printed sequence. The facilitator seeds a ripple by slowly opening and closing one hand once. Anyone who notices that movement may repeat it once after a comfortable pause; anyone noticing a repeat may do the same. No pointing, eye contact, assigned seats, or designated next person is needed. Overlapping ripples and their natural disappearance form a two-minute piece.

In the staff-permitted corner, the facilitator displays a card: “When you notice a hand open and close, you may repeat it once. Let it pass, or let it end. Watching is welcome. Stay seated if you wish.” The portable sign adds that boarding and announcements take priority. Gestures remain within personal space, without contact, clapping, or deliberate sound. The facilitator introduces at most three seeds, allowing each ripple to disappear before another.

The outcome changes through transmission between travelers: a gesture can reach someone who cannot continuously see the facilitator. This assumes some willing participants can see one another from existing seats. Sparse participation or ambiguous movements may prevent transmission; nobody is asked to fill a gap. Unlike the prior shared visual pulse, this permits uneven timing and disappearance, but adds uncertainty about which movements belong to the piece.

One facilitator owns setup, demonstration, stopping, and removal: three minutes to place materials, two minutes to perform, two minutes to clear. During announcements the facilitator displays a STOP card and lowers their hands; the sign instructs everyone to stop independently when an announcement begins. Restart requires a fresh seed.
EXPAND.experiment: In one reversible pilot, try a 30-second shared open-hand pulse, then up to one minute of ripples. Observe whether any gesture appears to travel beyond direct facilitator imitation, while checking for searching, conspicuous waiting, or pressure toward neighbors. Offer an optional printed question: “Did passing the gesture feel comfortable, or did following one leader feel easier?” Stop immediately for staff concern, interrupted attention to boarding, or circulation problems. If transmission is unclear or social pressure appears greater than with the simple pulse, the relay has shown no advantage; let it end and remove the materials.

EXPAND.title: The lounge chooses the next phrase
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: anonymous collective choices change the composition while it is happening. Participants help determine what comes next instead of simply executing a fixed score. The facilitator alternates a choice window with a short performed phrase. Two cards offer equally small, silent options: A—turn a palm upward and return; B—extend two fingers and relax. During the choice window, travelers may indicate A with one finger or B with two, held low within their own space. Abstaining and watching are explicitly welcome.

The facilitator scans only for a broad visible preference, names no individuals, and then shows the selected card. Everyone who wishes performs that gesture three times, following the facilitator’s slow movement. Three choice-and-performance rounds make a piece lasting about two minutes. If preference is unclear, the printed rule is “unclear means rest”: the facilitator models a quiet pause and proceeds to the next round. No exact count, explanation, or participation threshold is necessary.

Collective selection could give travelers a sense of authorship with very little instruction. Unlike the prior choose-your-own counter-rhythm, choices alter a shared subsequent phrase rather than produce independent overlapping cycles. The additional choice windows may nevertheless feel like voting pressure or make the rhythm too fragmented. It assumes the two cards and their labels are legible from existing seats; limited sightlines constrain both choosing and performing.

Use only printed cards and the portable sign in the approved corner. Allow three minutes for setup, two for performance, and two for removal by the single facilitator. The sign permits seated entry and departure at any moment, prohibits fixture contact, and gives announcements priority. Any announcement cancels the current round; the facilitator lowers their hands and resumes with a new choice only after it ends.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare one fixed 30-second phrase with two brief choice-and-performance rounds in the same pilot. The facilitator observes whether a choice can be understood without people approaching, calling out, or seeking individual acknowledgment. Offer the optional question: “Did choosing add enjoyment, or would simply following be more comfortable?” The route fails its comparison if choices remain ambiguous, reduce comfortable participation, or consume most of the activity without adding perceived authorship. Stop for staff concern, boarding interference, or audible discussion that competes with terminal information. Remove all materials immediately afterward; no continuing installation is needed.

EXPAND.title: A beat that continues out of sight
EXPAND.proposal:
Mechanism: a short visible rhythm establishes an internal pulse, followed by an interval in which participants sustain it privately. Continuous visual attention becomes unnecessary. A card reads: “Follow four slow hand openings. When the hands lower, imagine four more at the same pace. Tiny finger movements are optional. Then rest; look back only if you want another round.” Watching without joining is welcome.

The facilitator demonstrates four evenly spaced, small hand openings, then lowers both hands for approximately the same duration. Participants may continue the pulse mentally or with tiny movements above their lap, without touching seats, clothing, or fixtures. After a generous rest, the facilitator repeats the visible opening. Three rounds create a miniature with alternating visible and privately sustained sections. Returning together on an exact beat is unnecessary: each visible section is a fresh entry point, and travelers may join or leave anywhere.

This changes the need for sustained attention to a leader. The prior shared visual pulse requires ongoing sight of its timing reference; here, remembered timing carries part of the piece. That could suit travelers who need to glance at boarding information, although announcements always interrupt both imagined and physical participation. Mental timing may feel effortful, and its occurrence cannot be inferred from stillness. Participation therefore cannot be judged by visible coordination alone.

The only resources are the printed instruction card, portable sign, approved corner, and one facilitator. Allow three minutes for setup, two minutes for the piece, and two minutes to clear. Keep boarding signs and circulation fully visible. The sign states that announcements end the current round immediately; the facilitator models stopping. A new round begins only after the announcement, with four fresh visible gestures. No eyes-closed exercise, controlled breathing, or individual demonstration is requested.
EXPAND.experiment: Try one continuously visible round and one round containing the private continuation, each under 30 seconds. Observe whether instructions cause repeated checking, visible strain, or approaches to the sign. Offer the optional question: “Was continuing privately comfortable, or was watching throughout easier?” A report that the internal section felt like a memory test counts against it, even if movement looks coordinated. Stop for staff concern or competing attention during boarding. If nobody volunteers feedback, comfort and internal participation remain unknown; do not treat stillness as success. End after the bounded trial and clear the corner.

EXPAND.title: A shared pulse with a seated visibility gate
EXPAND.proposal:
Source: “A shared visual pulse.” Preserve the facilitator-led four-beat phrase—open palm, close palm, open palm, rest—and add an operational visibility check before inviting participation. The facilitator places the printed instruction card and portable sign in the staff-permitted corner, then checks them from the existing seats the activity would serve. Proceed only where the instructions and small gestures are discernible without leaning, approaching, or obscuring boarding information. One repositioning within the permitted corner is allowed; if it fails, remove the materials and cancel this session. Do not recruit travelers to better seats.

The sign reads: “Quiet rhythm. Watch or join, seated or standing. Small finger movements welcome. Leave or stop anytime. Pause immediately for announcements.” Run a two-minute phrase with no individual invitations, corrections, clapping, snapping, fixture contact, or amplification. The facilitator lowers both hands during announcements and starts a fresh phrase afterward. Setup and visibility checking take at most three minutes, the piece two minutes, optional feedback one minute, and clearance two minutes, all managed by one facilitator.

The changed action prevents a foreseeable failure of the source’s central prerequisite: a usable common visual reference. Compared with proceeding directly, it costs a brief walk through existing seating and may cancel an otherwise possible session. It could reduce crowding and strained viewing, but cannot establish visual accessibility for everyone.
EXPAND.experiment: Run one reversible session only after the visibility gate passes. The facilitator observes whether willing participants follow from their seats, approach to decipher instructions, or repeatedly lean or search. Stop if participation requires approaching, if staff identify an access or distraction problem, or if boarding signs become obscured. Offer the optional question, without addressing anyone individually: “Was this comfortable to watch or join from your seat?” Visible coordination is evidence about timing, not comfort. If visibility fails during use, end and clear rather than enlarge the activity. No feedback leaves comfort uncertain.

EXPAND.title: A printed miniature with restartable sections
EXPAND.proposal:
Source: “A rhythm read across the page.” Preserve private, self-paced reading of a printed gesture score, but divide the score into two clearly boxed, independently playable sections. Box A reads “open hand, rest, two fingers, rest”; box B reads “open hand, two fingers, rest, rest.” Each symbol has a text label. Add: “Choose either box. Read slowly at your own pace. Repeat or change boxes whenever you wish. If interrupted or you lose your place, stop; restart at the beginning of either box only when ready.”

This gives the participant responsibility for restarting without remembering a position, catching up, or waiting for the facilitator. Announcements end the current reading immediately. Afterward, either box is a complete new entry point. The facilitator silently demonstrates one box once; travelers may join, watch, or leave unnoticed throughout a three-minute window, using tiny movements above their laps while seated. No deliberate sound, fixture contact, or amplification is involved.

The facilitator uses only printed cards, the portable sign, and the permitted corner. Allow three minutes for setup and a seated readability check, three for participation and optional feedback, and two for clearance. Keep signs and circulation clear. If the score cannot be read from existing seats, cancel and remove it. Compared with the source’s uninterrupted eight-symbol reading, the changed recovery procedure reduces place-keeping demands but sacrifices some longer musical phrasing and adds two short instructions. Its value depends on those instructions remaining legible and simple.
EXPAND.experiment: In one session, offer the two restartable boxes and demonstrate stopping midway, resting, then beginning either box again. Do not manufacture a terminal announcement. The facilitator observes whether willing readers use complete short phrases without approaching the card or seeking help; natural interruptions may provide additional evidence but are not required. Offer: “Was it comfortable to stop and begin again, or did the boxes make the card harder to follow?” End if reading causes crowding, visible strain, or attention problems identified by staff. If the restart rule confuses participants, stop the pilot and clear; do not introduce another explanation during boarding. Without feedback, the recovery benefit remains unconfirmed.

EXPAND.title: Two halves make a quiet rhythm
EXPAND.proposal:
New mechanism: complementary parts create a visual hocket—a rhythm distributed between participants. Unlike independent overlapping patterns, each part deliberately leaves spaces for the other. Two printed cards show A: “open, rest, open, rest” and B: “rest, open, rest, open.” Travelers silently choose either part and may change, stop, or watch at any time. There are no assigned groups, partners, seats, or obligations to fill a missing part.

The facilitator holds the labeled A and B cards apart within a small personal space, alternately lifting each card slowly. Participants choosing that letter briefly open one hand when its card rises, then relax. Seated finger extension is an equivalent option. Four alternating lifts followed by a generous rest form one phrase; repeat for up to two minutes. If only one part is taken, its alternating movement and rests remain a complete acceptable piece. The facilitator never asks anyone to supply the other part.

The working principle is complementary omission: separate contributions can reveal an alternating whole without interaction between strangers. It assumes the two letters and cue movements are visible from existing seats. Compared with everyone copying one pulse, it may make collective participation more perceptible, but adds a part-selection burden and divides visual attention. This benefit is untested.

One facilitator sets up and checks seated visibility in three minutes, performs for two, offers optional feedback for one, and clears in two. Use only the permitted corner, cards, and portable sign. The sign permits anonymous entry and departure, gives announcements priority, and prohibits deliberate sound and fixture contact. Both cards lower immediately for announcements; afterward a fresh phrase starts. If cues are illegible or obstruct information, cancel rather than move travelers.
EXPAND.experiment: Pilot a short demonstration followed by three or four alternating phrases. The facilitator observes whether willing participants distinguish the parts without approaching, speaking, or looking for individual acknowledgment. Sparse participation is acceptable and does not trigger recruitment. Offer the optional question: “Was choosing one half comfortable, or would following the same movement be easier?” Stop and clear for staff concern, obstructed information, circulation interference, or persistent confusion between the two cues. Judge the idea against the simple shared pulse on understandable rhythm and reported comfort, including the extra attention required to track a letter. Do not infer that both parts were understood merely because hands moved.
